cases.input: After that help, here is the next part of my reasoning to examine: I can distinguish a count of bits from a count of packets, but I still do not see why a packet with more bits would occupy the sender for longer at a fixed bit rate. Could you give a different, non-numerical way to think about that interval without answering the current cable-length question? I am asking for help, not submitting an answer.

content.text: Imagine a strip of time at the sender, with each bit occupying an equal-width slot. A fixed bit rate keeps those slots the same width. A packet with more bits needs more slots, so its strip extends longer before the sender has placed its last bit onto the link. That first-to-last-bit sending interval is transmission delay.

proposal.reason_summary: The student requests a different, non-numerical explanation of why more bits require a longer sending interval at a fixed bit rate. cases.input: Before answering the lesson question, I want help examining my mental picture. I imagine that all the bits of a packet are placed on the link at the same instant, and then the whole packet travels together. I cannot tell what the transmission interval is measuring in that picture. Please help me inspect it without solving the active question; this is not an assessed answer.

content.text: To inspect your picture, focus just on the sending end. Picture a timeline with each bit occupying a small interval, rather than all bits being placed on the link at once. The transmission interval measures the time needed to put the packet’s bits onto the link—from beginning the first bit to finishing the last. It is not timing the packet’s journey along the cable. Try marking those two endpoints on your mental timeline, leaving the cable-length question aside.
